title: “Google and Reddit do not own the Internet," web scraper says after court win
gist: A court dismissed Google's DMCA lawsuit against web-scraper SerpApi for lack of standing over uncopyrightable search results, weakening a parallel Reddit suit against SerpApi and Perplexity and spotlighting a broader industry push by platforms to legally wall off scraping of the open web.

insights.claim: Google sued web scraper SerpApi in December, invoking the DMCA and accusing it of circumventing Google's anti-scraping technology to sell scraped search-result content through an unauthorized "Google Search API" service.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Shows Google is willing to litigate aggressively against third-party search-data resellers, raising legal risk for any company building products on scraped Google search results.
insights.locator: Curiously invoking the Digital Millennium Copyright Act

insights.claim: Google's DMCA theory was legally unusual because Google search results themselves cannot be copyrighted, so Google instead argued its anti-scraping tech protects copyrighted content licensed into its 'knowledge panels.'
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The novelty and narrowness of this legal theory signals uncertain, evolving case law around scraping public search data.
insights.quote: Google search results can’t be copyrighted
insights.locator: It was an odd use of the DMCA

insights.claim: Google explicitly cited Reddit's earlier October lawsuit against SerpApi and Perplexity as precedent when announcing its own DMCA challenge against SerpApi.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Suggests a copycat legal playbook among major content platforms against AI scrapers that other publishers could replicate.
insights.locator: In a blog, Google cited Reddit’s lawsuit

insights.claim: Reddit sued SerpApi and Perplexity in October, alleging they evaded two layers of security -- Reddit's own anti-scraping controls and Google's controls blocking scraping of Reddit content within search results.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Reddit is actively litigating to protect the value of its content licensing business against unlicensed AI-era scraping.
insights.locator: Reddit filed a very similar lawsuit in October

insights.claim: SerpApi accuses Reddit of trying to act as a 'toll collector' over content it doesn't own, framing Reddit's lawsuit as an attempt to tax scraped content rather than protect its users.
insights.speaker: SerpApi
insights.so_what: Frames Reddit's litigation as monetization strategy for its data-licensing business, a lens investors can apply when assessing Reddit's AI-data revenue ambitions.
insights.quote: Reddit seeks to consolidate its control over its users’ content so that it will be in a better position to tax that content. Reddit is not acting to protect its users; Reddit is clearing a path to exploit them.
insights.locator: In a win, SerpApi warned that Reddit planned to act as a “toll collector,”

insights.claim: Advance Publications, which owns Ars Technica parent Condé Nast, is the largest shareholder in Reddit.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A disclosed conflict of interest: Ars Technica's ultimate owner has a direct financial stake in the outcome of the Reddit litigation it is covering.
insights.locator: Advance Publications, which owns Ars Technica parent

insights.claim: A court granted SerpApi's motion to dismiss early in Google's lawsuit, ruling Google lacked DMCA standing because it didn't own the content in its search results and hadn't shown it was acting on behalf of any rights holder.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Sets an early legal precedent limiting platforms' ability to use DMCA claims against companies scraping public search results.
insights.quote: That does not happen terribly often
insights.locator: Last week, a court took the somewhat rare step

insights.claim: Policy counsel Meredith Rose says the Google ruling bodes poorly for Reddit's parallel case against SerpApi, since Reddit similarly cannot claim to be the copyright owner or exclusive licensee of content appearing in search results.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Increases the probability Reddit's suit against SerpApi and Perplexity is also dismissed, reducing legal risk for scraping-dependent data companies.
insights.quote: Reddit is none of those things.
insights.locator: Likely the timing of that decision wasn’t great for Reddit

insights.claim: In Reddit's hearing on SerpApi's motion to dismiss, the judge appeared most focused on whether Reddit's agreement with Google actually authorized Google to protect Reddit's copyrighted content on its behalf.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The Reddit-Google authorization agreement is now the single pivotal legal question that will decide whether Reddit's case survives.
insights.locator: Most particularly, the judge seemed interested

insights.claim: Google was given 21 days to amend its complaint and plans to argue that rights holders directly authorized it to use anti-scraping technology to protect copyrighted content within knowledge panels.
insights.speaker: José Castañeda
insights.so_what: Watch for Google's amended complaint around mid-to-late August 2026; its success determines whether Google retains any DMCA leverage against scrapers.
insights.quote: We look forward to filing an amended complaint, as the Court invited us to do, and we remain committed to protecting our services and partners from unauthorized access.
insights.locator: Google acknowledged that search results can’t be copyrighted

insights.claim: Rose argues Google faces a legal trap: to prove its knowledge panels contain copyrighted material, Google must concede that only its explicitly licensed content is protected, implicitly admitting the rest of the algorithmically generated knowledge box has been reproduced without a license and could face a separate fair-use challenge.
insights.speaker: Meredith Rose
insights.so_what: Google's narrowed legal strategy risks opening it up to a bigger copyright/fair-use liability around automated knowledge-panel generation.
insights.quote: Otherwise, they’re admitting that they have been reproducing stuff without licensing it, and that gets them into another fair use fight that they probably don’t want to have.
insights.locator: For Google, it could be “very dangerous”

insights.claim: SerpApi's paying customers include Nvidia, Uber, and Adobe, and the company says its business has continued to grow throughout the Google and Reddit litigation despite the resulting customer uncertainty.
insights.speaker: SerpApi
insights.so_what: Demonstrates real enterprise demand for structured search-data access even under active legal attack, a proof point for the scraping-as-a-service data market.
insights.quote: rely on SerpApi every day to provide structured access to search data, which is and has always been a lawful and legitimate business
insights.locator: SerpApi told Ars that its business has continued to grow

insights.claim: SerpApi frames both the Google and Reddit lawsuits as attempts to wall off the open Internet by retroactively claiming control over content the platforms neither authored nor own.
insights.speaker: SerpApi
insights.so_what: Signals SerpApi's public-interest litigation strategy and messaging, positioning itself as a defender of open-web data access for the wider AI/data industry.
insights.quote: The bottom line is that both Google and Reddit appear to be engaged in attempts to use the DMCA to wall off the open Internet by retroactively claiming control over content that they didn’t author and don’t own.
insights.locator: SerpApi is hoping that the fight will be over soon

insights.claim: SerpApi accuses Google of hypocrisy, calling it the 'largest scraper on the planet' while seeking to cut off rival scrapers from search data that is '100 percent public.'
insights.speaker: SerpApi
insights.so_what: Highlights a competitive-dynamics angle: Google's own scale as a scraper undercuts its legal narrative and could be used against it in later proceedings.
insights.locator: Similarly, SerpApi accused Google of asking the court

insights.claim: Rose dates the shift toward locking down open-web access to the summer of 2023's 'API apocalypse,' when publishers began broadly restricting access in reaction to the rise of AI scraping.
insights.speaker: Meredith Rose
insights.so_what: Marks a three-year structural trend of publishers closing off data access, relevant context for any AI company dependent on open-web crawling as a training input.

insights.claim: Rose warns the mass reaction to AI scraping is causing a 're-enclosure' of large parts of the web, which harms not just AI training but also research, archiving, journalism, and public-health reporting that depend on open automated crawling.
insights.speaker: Meredith Rose
insights.so_what: A structural, cross-industry risk factor for any business or research effort that depends on open-web crawling as a data source, not just AI labs.
insights.quote: re-enclosure of a lot of the web

insights.claim: Rose predicts DMCA copyright litigation outcomes remain hard to forecast because rulings in the copyright realm can be inconsistent and subjective across judges.
insights.speaker: Meredith Rose
insights.so_what: Legal uncertainty around AI-scraping litigation broadly is a persistent risk factor for the sector, beyond just this case's outcome.
insights.quote: whenever you get into the copyright realm, a lot of judges just decide it’s all vibes
insights.locator: And although SerpApi expects to win
